Fire Facts
• Almost 20% of home fire deaths resulted from fires 
beginning with upholstered furniture
• Over 40% of home fires are caused by cooking 
equipment
• Fire safety systems here on Earth have been developed 
based on extensive study of typical fires
• Established body of research characterizes smoke from 
building fires and forest fires (flaming combustion)
• Current fire detection systems in space were developed 
without spacecraft fire data
• International Space Station has no cooking, no couches that 
can catch on fire

typical spacecraft materials

chunks.title: Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors
chunks.text:
Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors David L. Urban, Gary Ruff: NASA Glenn Research Center 
Zeng-guang Yuan:  National Center for Space Exploration Research 
Thomas Cleary, Jiann Yang and George Mulholland National Institute of Standards and Technology Rapid fire detection requires the ability to differentiate fire signatures from background conditions and 
nuisance sources. Proper design of a fire detector requires detailed knowledge of all of these signal 
sources so that a discriminating detector can be designed. Owing to the absence of microgravity smoke 
data, all current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed based upon normal-g conditions. The 
removal of buoyancy reduces the velocities in the high temperature zones in flames, increasing the 
residence time of smoke particles and consequently allowing longer growth time for the particles.

chunks.title: Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors
chunks.text:
Recent space shuttle experiments confirmed that, in some cases, increased particles sizes are seen in 
low-gravity and that the relative performance of the ISS (International Space Station) and space-shuttle 
smoke-detectors changes in low-gravity; however, sufficient particle size information to design new 
detectors was not obtained. To address this issue, the SAME (Smoke Aerosol Measurement 
Experiment) experiment is manifested to fly on the ISS in 2007. The SAME experiment will make 
measurements of the particle size distribution of the smoke particulate from several typical spacecraft 
materials providing quantitative design data for spacecraft smoke detectors. A precursor experiment 
(DAFT: Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test) flew recently on the ISS and provided the first 
measurement of the background smoke particulate levels on the ISS.

chunks.title: Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors
chunks.text:
These background levels are 
critical to the design of future smoke detectors. The ISS cabin was found to be a very clean 
environment with particulate levels substantially below the space shuttle and typical ground-based 
environments.

Background: Spacecraft Fire 
Detection
• Fire detection strategies for spacecraft have largely 
been based upon 1-g understanding.
• Soot particle size distributions are larger in μ-g flames.
(work of Ku, Faeth and Choi)
• Results from a limited data set of μ-g smoke 
particulate suggest that smoke particle sizes are 
substantially larger for both solid and liquid smoke 
aerosols (McKinnon and Apostalakis)
• Proper design of spacecraft fire detection systems will 
require measurements of the particle size distributions 
of typical μ-g smoke sources.

Background: Spacecraft Fire Detection
• Developed in the late 70’s when Ionization detectors were 
prevalent
•Limited 1-g testing supported small particle size distribution for 
incipient fires 
•Detector was designed to reject particles with aerodynamic 
diameters greater than 1-2 microns.
• Decades of service with very few false alarms and no alarms. STS Detector:  sensitive < 1 micron
•dual-chamber ionization detector 
•vane pump provides inertial separation system
•designed to make the detector insensitive to 
particulate larger than 1 to 2μm
•fairly large power consumption (9 Watts)
•fan noise and limited life due to the moving parts
•Installed in avionics air returns (possible reason for 
fan)

Residential (1-g) background
Well ventilated flames and established fires emit smaller 
particulate with sizes readily detected by ionization 
detectors 
• Smoldering fires and over-heated (pyrolyzing) materials 
produce larger particulate favoring scattering detectors. • Ionization detectors were favored in the 1970’s though the 
mid 1990’s due to the difficulty of producing light sources 
that would remain stable for several years. • The advent of improvements in light emitting diode and 
diode laser technology has reduced the cost and increased 
the stability of photoelectric fire detectors.

chunks.text:
www.nasa.gov17/30
SAME Experiment
• CSD demonstrated
– Smoke detector design must be based on low-g data
– Liquid smoke aerosols require on-orbit measurement of 
smoke particulate size distribution
• Power and mass limitations prevent direct 
measurement of the smoke particle size 
distribution
• Integral measures (moments) of the particle size 
distribution were chosen as the best approach 
• SAME (Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment) 
Shipped and ready for launch this summer

chunks.title: Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors
chunks.text:
www.nasa.gov18/30
SAME 
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment
Motivation
• Droplet size for liquid-smoke aerosols are essentially 
unknown.
• Particulate dimensions for solid-particulate smoke have 
been measured for a small number of particles. Despite its demonstrated effectiveness, smoke detection has 
remaining challenges for spacecraft:
– Increased importance on longer missions
– The current state of knowledge is insufficient to truly 
assure system effectiveness. – Rational design and implementation require better smoke 
particulate size distribution information.
This research will directly improve crew safety and mission 
assurance by providing data necessary to ensure reliable 
detection of incipient spacecraft fires, ensuring the safety of 
future crews and missions.

chunks.title: Linking Remotely Sensed Aerosol Types to Their Chemical Composition
chunks.text:
Johnson, M 
NCTS# 25415-17 AGU 2016 Linking remotely sensed aerosol types to their chemical composition Aerosol types measured during the Ship-Aircraft Bio-Optical Research (SABOR) 
experiment are related to GEOS-Chem model chemical composition. The application for 
this procedure to link model chemical components to aerosol type is desirable for 
understanding aerosol evolution over time. The Mahalanobis distance (DM) statistic is 
used to cluster model groupings of five chemical components (organic carbon, black 
carbon, sea salt, dust and sulfate) in a way analogous to the methods used by Burton et al.

chunks.title: Linking Remotely Sensed Aerosol Types to Their Chemical Composition
chunks.text:
[2012] and Russell et al. [2014]. First, model-to-measurement evaluation is performed by 
collocating vertically resolved aerosol extinction from SABOR High Spectral Resolution 
LiDAR (HSRL) to the GEOS-Chem nested high-resolution data. Comparisons of 
modeled-to-measured aerosol extinction are shown to be within 35% ± 14%. Second, the 
model chemical components are calculation into five variables to calculate the DM and 
cluster means and covariances for each HSRL-retrieved aerosol type. The layer variables 
from the model are aerosol optical depth (AOD) ratios of (i) sea salt and (ii) dust to total 
AOD, mass ratios of (iii) total carbon (i.e. sum of organic and black carbon) to the sum of 
total carbon and sulfate (iv) organic carbon to black carbon, and (v) the natural log of the 
aerosol-to-molecular extinction ratio. Third, the layer variables and at most five out of 
twenty SABOR

chunks.title: Linking Remotely Sensed Aerosol Types to Their Chemical Composition
chunks.text:
black carbon, and (v) the natural log of the 
aerosol-to-molecular extinction ratio. Third, the layer variables and at most five out of 
twenty SABOR flights are used to form the pre-specified clusters for calculating DM and 
to assign an aerosol type. After determining the pre-specified clusters, model aerosol 
types are produced for the entire vertically resolved GEOS-Chem nested domain over the 
United States and the model chemical component distributions relating to each type are 
recorded. Resulting aerosol types are Dust/Dusty Mix, Maritime, Smoke, Urban and 
Fresh Smoke (separated into ‘dark’ and ‘light’ by a threshold of the organic to black 
carbon ratio). Model-calculated DM not belonging to a specific type (i.e. not meeting a 
threshold probability) is termed an outlier and those DM values that can belong to 
multiple types (i.e. showing weak probability of belonging to a spec

chunks.title: Linking Remotely Sensed Aerosol Types to Their Chemical Composition
chunks.text:
reshold probability) is termed an outlier and those DM values that can belong to 
multiple types (i.e. showing weak probability of belonging to a specific cluster) are 
termed as Overlap. MODIS active fires are overlaid on the model domain to qualitatively 
evaluate the model-predicted Smoke aerosol types.

• For spacecraft materials, number counts decreased by a 
factor of 1.7 to 2.7 over 800 seconds. • The measured and predicted number decreases agree within 
about 20 %. • The best agreement between experiment and prediction is 
Davm - agree within 4 %. • The decrease in the geometric standard deviation is typically 
more than a factor of two greater than the predicted change. • Aging results are relevant to partially sealed volumes and 
low air flow  conditions. • In all cases, aging resulted in approximately a factor of two 
decrease in number concentration and a factor of two

chunks.title: Particle Morphology Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
chunks.text:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration 
www.nasa.gov 
 32 
Conclusions 
• For the conditions tested, the materials emit most 
of their particulate in the submicron range. • The ISS detector showed a relatively weak signal 
for some Teflon runs doubtless a result of the 
particle size. • Particle morphology varies widely across the 
range of expected sample materials. Dependence 
on a single angle scattering device will be 
difficult. • Aging results consistent with theory for number 
count and Davm but not for σg

chunks.title: Particle Morphology Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
chunks.text:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration 
www.nasa.gov 
 33 
Implications and Future Work 
• Dust rejection may be achievable by detecting at 
the sub-micron level. • Given the effects of aging and the slow mixing 
seen in spacecraft, it is probably unwise to focus 
entirely on small particle sizes for fire detection 
• Size selective smoke detection will improve 
reliability and false alarm rejection. Either by 
classifying the particles or by measuring multiple 
moments.

The Summer of ‘91: Baie Commeau or Pinatubo? The enhanced aerosol in the northern hemi-
sphere Summer of 1991 (seen below) has been 
attributed to fresh aerosol from Mt Pinatubo 
(Thomason et al., 1992) and to smoke from a 
forest /f_ire in Quebec (Baie Commeau) (Fromm et 
al, 2012). The plot collection below shows data 
from 1991 with some additional 30-day ratio 
scatter plots for clarity. It is clear that this set of 
data is considerably diﬀerent from any smoke 
event seen in either SAGE II or SAGE III period 
with a large clump of data in the HEHR zone that 
increases in frequency through out the period 
shown (and is mostly lost by December as dense 
Pinatubo aerosol moves from the tropics and 
obscures the lower stratosphere for next few 
years. This cluster forms initially at an extinction 
~0.001/km and a ratio of ~5 and then slowly 
moves its center to 0.002/km and a ratio ~3.

where the ratio either is pushed toward 1 at

havior is, however, consistent with low density,

this clump originates from one of the Pinatubo 
eruptions, either the main event or one of the 
lesser  eruptions prior to that and that less dense 
portions of the volcanic injection mostly below 20 km were transported to the NH as this aerosol formed. Still, Fromm et al.

mostly occurred during a period of relatively low aerosol

chunks.text:
pheric Aerosol and Gas Experiment aboard the International Space Station (SAGE III/ISS) has 
mostly occurred during a period of relatively low aerosol loading. At the same time, it has almost observed a number 
of small to moderate injections of volcanic material in the stratosphere from the Aoba/Ambae eruption of 2018 to 
that of Karymsky in 2022. In addition, two of the largest known smoke intrusions into the stratosphere have occurred 
during the SAGE III/ISS mission (the British Columbia /f_ire of August 2017 and the Australian Wild/f_ire Event of 2019/2020).

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
At least two other much smaller smoke events have also been observed in the SAGE III data (California Creek in 
September 2020 and McKay Creek in June 2021). Particularly with the two large events, it is tempting to speculate that these events are increasing in intensity and frequen-
cy possibly due to ongoing climate change. Realistically, change is diﬃcult to assess since instrument data sets that can 
be used for quantifying historical events can be quite diﬀerent in what and where they provide measurements.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
This com-
plicates comparing one event to another potentially separated by many years. An exception to this issues are the mea-
suremens by SAGE III/ISS and those of its predecessor SAGE II (1984-2005). Both use the same measurement strategy, 
measure aerosol extinction coeﬃcient at 1020 nm, and have similar spatial/temporal coverage. Both instruments are 
known to observe smoke events in the stratosphere. However, both have the same low observation density characteristic 
of solar occultation such that near-global coverage takes almost a month and characterizing 
eﬀectively instant events like smoke and volcanic events take a matter of weeks depending 
on the vagaries of where the observations are being made at a critical juncture unlike instru-
ments with high temporal/spatial resolution like limb-scatter instruments such as OMPS and 
OSIRIS. The goal of this work will be to use the sa

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
nstru-
ments with high temporal/spatial resolution like limb-scatter instruments such as OMPS and 
OSIRIS. The goal of this work will be to use the same analysis approach to both the SAGE II and 
SAGE III data and compare both the frequency and intensity of smoke events observed by 
these instruments. While we do not expect to be able to make conclusions about change be-
tween the periods, the analysis is a /f_irst step in interpreting changes in the contribution of 
smoke to the stratospheric aerosol budget between the time frames encompassed by these 
instruments.
Generally Morphology of the SAGE III/ISS and SAGE II measurements
    The images below show mean 1020-nm aerosol extinction coeﬃcient in 3 broad latitude 
bands  30-70 N and S and 20N to 20S in monthly medians with a 3-month window for the 
SAGE III life time (above) and SAGE II’s (below). This approach maintains step discont

chunks.text:
nd 20N to 20S in monthly medians with a 3-month window for the 
SAGE III life time (above) and SAGE II’s (below). This approach maintains step discontinuities 
and minimize the eﬀect of occasional outliers in the data (mostly due to the presence of cloud 
in the lower stratosphere despite only using data at least 2 km above the MERRA tropopause.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
All Things Color Bar
    The tropical analyses of both data sets is clearly dominated by volcanic activity with a number of smallish events in the SAGE III record with 
relatively fewer but much stronger events in the SAGE II record. Similarly, the higher latitudes show impacts from low and high latitude erup-
tions. On the other hand, two large smoke events in the SAGE III record (BC, 2017 and Australia, 2020) clearly show in the SAGE III record in a 
manner similar to mid-size volcanic events, impulse followed by recovery, whereas smoke impacts in the SAGE II record are diﬃcult to discern 
in this scale of plot but can be noted for some events such (Norman Wells in 1998) as transient increases.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
To the left are 10 instances where we have identi/f_ied clear instances of smoke in the stratosphere in the SAGE II and III data sets. Each 
instance consists of 7 images that depict various aspects of these events. It should be noted, that since we expect smoke and clouds to have 
similar optical signatures, we exclude data within 2 km of the reported tropopause height. In addition, we only look for signi/f_icant clusters of 
enhanced aerosol extinction (1020 nm) and thus isolated outliers are not considered. Overall, this approach may decrease the magnitude and 
pervasiveness of smoke events, but there is little recourse based  to broaden the analysis. Due to high aerosol levels prior to 1986 and from mid 
1991 through 1994, we did not closely examine these periods for smoke events.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
The presence of smoke is inferred by the presence of extinction enhancements at 1020 nm and knowledge of strong /f_ire events having oc-
curred (as opposed to volcanic activity). Seasonality is also relevant particularly in the southern hemisphere as the presence of polar strato-
spheric clouds in the lower stratosphere frequently occur particularly in the SAGE II data. For each smoke event, the upper right image shows 
the scatter of extinction coeﬃcient in the broad latitude band (30-70 either N or S) at the altitude where the presence of outliers was most ap-
parent. These are highlighted by ellipses. While individual extinction observations may be quite enhanced over the local background level, 
most events do not dominate frequency of occurrence even at there most wide spread.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
This is also clear in the mean extinction coeﬃcient 
plots (upper left) where some events are diﬃcult to see in the zonal average. It is really only the two large events (British Columbia, 2017 and 
Australia, 2020) that clearly and in a sustained way enhance the zonally averages aerosol extinction coeﬃcient (in both upper plots) and so 
none in the SAGE II period. The center sets of 3 plots show the scatter of all data points in the stratosphere for 30 day periods spanning the initial appearance of en-
hanced aerosol in the stratosphere which we associate with smoke.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
The /f_irst plot covers period just prior to the event and from this data we 
determine the 99.5-percentile extinction value (shown as a vertical line in all plots) above which data is considered to be enhanced. In addition 
for extinction values above the 50-percentile, we compute the mean extinction coeﬃcient ratio (525/1020) (eﬀectively the mean ratio for the 
central cluster of extinction) and show this as a horizontal line in all plots. We use the two quadrants on the enhanced aerosol side of these 
plots to crudely divide the data into a high extinction/high ratio (HEHR) region and a high extinction/low ratio region (or CLASP explained 
below).

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
It is clear that for all 10 of these events, that the enhanced aerosol observations lie almost entirely in the CLASP region with most 
showing a decreasing extinction ratio for increasing extinction ratio. This makes sense for smoke-related aerosol since it is likely highly absorb-
ing at all SAGE wavelengths and would tend to exhibit a /f_lat spectral dependence. This is modulated by the /f_ield-of-view mixing of ambient 
sulfuric acid aerosol and smoke so appearing in SAGE data as a continuum in ratio rather than two distinct clusters. This separation method  is 
pretty crude and some mixing of identi/f_ications is expected particularly for marginally enhanced extinction coeﬃcient.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
We refer to a CLASP 
region in recognition that SAGE data cannot separate between some aerosol compositions uniquely based solely on extinction coeﬃcient and 
it spectral ratio. There are a number of aerosol compositions that can produce low extinction ratio include Clouds, Large sulfuric acid aerosol, 
Ash, Smoke and ice PSCs producing CLASP . That cloud and smoke can look similar suggests some concern for GloSSAC as cloud clearing is a 
necessary component of that analysis while retaining all kinds of other aerosol is a priority. Ash is a frequent component of volcanic eruptions 
and, particularly for smaller eruptions, occasionally dominate the optical signature at some altitudes. Large volcanic events can produce large 
sulfuric acid aerosol which have small extinction ratios (see Mt. Pinatubo for instance). PSCs are not observed in the SAGE III data but are 
common in the southern h

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
rosol which have small extinction ratios (see Mt. Pinatubo for instance). PSCs are not observed in the SAGE III data but are 
common in the southern hemisphere winter. Separating between these types of aerosol, to the degree that they can, is most often based on 
context (external knowledge of potential events of interest, season, altitude, etc.). The lower pair of /f_igures show the frequency of occurrence 
of the two categories.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
The diﬀerence between the two large events  and the others in frequency of occurrence is particularly apparent as the 
frequency of CLASP events approaches 100% and persists for months afterward. Whereas the smaller events perhaps transiently approach sim-
ilar frequencies but do not persist beyond a few months. To quantify the enhancements for these events we use a the enhancement in column optical depth. However, since many of these smoke 
events do not span vertically appreciably (and other altitudes may be increasing or decreasing for independent reasons), we only compute the 
vertical column enhancement over the altitude where CLASP is non-zero (and contiguous). The resulting enhancements are shown in the table 
below.

chunks.title: A Comparison of Stratospheric Smoke Events Seen by SAGE II (1984-2005) and SAGE III (2017-2021)
chunks.text:
Unsurprisingly, the Australian /f_ires of 2020 are by far the largest of these events and more than 3 times the next largest event (BC, 2017) 
and almost 5 times the largest SAGE II event (Norman Wells, 1998). Over all, these are rate events with only 10 over almost 20 years of 
SAGE-like observations thus inferring change between the periods is for more optimistic period than this author. It is clear that particularly the 
Australian event is a substantial outlier among these events and further developments should be interesting.
